texto:
Amazon's window for sellers to submit Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals closes today, October 20, 2026, according to a Seller News post the company published on October 8. The post, filed under the "Grow Your Business" category, pairs the deadline with a four-item checklist covering Account Health Rating, deal health status, listing quality, and payment and tax settings - the conditions Amazon lists as standing between a submitted deal and one that actually runs.
In Short
Amazon lets independent sellers sign up discounts to appear during its Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales, and the last day to sign them up is today. Sellers who miss it cannot get new deals into those events through this window, and the deals they did submit can still fail if their account, listings or tax details have problems. Amazon's notice lists four things to check, and a consultant's LinkedIn post repeated them with more detail on what usually goes wrong.
What the October 8 notice says
The post carries the headline "Submit your Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals before October 20." Its opening sentence states the date plainly: according to Amazon, "The submission window for Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals closes October 20, 2026." The post goes on to describe the event as reaching "millions of ready-to-buy customers at peak holiday demand," without putting a number on that audience.
Three reasons for submitting early follow, each bolded in the original. Under "Secure stronger placement," Amazon writes that "Early movers get better deal visibility and placement, so submitting ahead of the deadline helps your products get seen." Under "Capture peak holiday demand," the company calls the period "one of the highest-traffic shopping moments of the year." Under "Act on personalized recommendations," it says event deal recommendations "are tailored to your catalog's performance data, so you can prioritize the products most likely to convert."
None of these claims comes with a mechanism or a figure. The post does not explain how submission timing translates into placement, how much better visibility early submitters receive, or which performance data feeds the recommendations. A screenshot of the post captured for this article showed 4.2K views and six likes; the capture is undated, so those counts reflect an unknown point between October 8 and today.
The post closes by directing sellers to "review your personalized recommendations and submit your deals in the Deals dashboard before October 20." The words "Deals dashboard" appear as link text in the screenshot, but the image does not show the destination URL, so this article cannot confirm where the link points. Inside Seller Central, Amazon's interface for third-party sellers, deals sit under the Advertising menu.
The four checks
The second half of the post is a checklist. According to Amazon, the items are:
- Account Health Rating: "resolve any policy warnings or violations."
- Deal health status: "fix any suppressed or at-risk deals."
- Listing quality: "Ensure all deal-linked listings are active and meet quality requirements."
- Payment and tax settings: "Verify your payment and tax settings are current and complete."
The list is short and generic. It does not define what threshold of Account Health Rating blocks a deal, what qualifies a deal as "at-risk," or which quality requirements apply to deal-linked listings. Nor does it say whether a deal that fails one of these checks after the deadline can be repaired and kept in the event, or whether it drops out entirely. Those gaps matter on the last day of the window, when a seller discovering a suppressed deal has hours rather than weeks to act.
What the notice does establish is that submission alone is not the finish line. A deal sitting in the dashboard can still be suppressed, and the post treats account standing, listing status and back-office settings as preconditions for a deal to go live.
A deadline set in July
October 8 was not the first time the date appeared. When Amazon published its 2026 holiday calendar in July, the Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday submission window was set to run from July 8 to October 20, 2026. The October post is a reminder of a deadline that had been public for more than three months.
The fees attached to these deals are not mentioned in the October 8 post. PPC Land's July reporting put them at a $100 upfront fee per promotion plus 1.5% of promotional sales, capped at $5,000, for Best Deals, Lightning Deals and Prime Exclusive Price Discounts. Sellers who submitted by September 5 saved $50 on the upfront portion of each deal. That reduction expired more than six weeks ago, so every deal entered in the final stretch carries the full upfront fee.
How does that compare with ordinary weeks? PPC Land's explainer on the lightning deal format lists the non-peak US fee since June 2, 2025 as $70 per day plus 1.0% of deal sales, with the variable part capped at $2,000. Before June 2025, sellers paid a flat $150 per deal on ordinary days and $500 at peak events. Under the current model, the peak premium sits mostly in the higher percentage and the higher cap rather than in a fixed charge.
The holiday calendar runs well beyond today. According to PPC Land's coverage of the inbound deadlines for Amazon's 2026 holiday events, the Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday cutoffs are October 14 for Amazon Warehousing and Distribution, October 21 for FBA shipments with minimal splits and October 28 for FBA shipments with Amazon-optimized splits. Peak fulfillment fees apply from October 15, 2026 to January 14, 2027, at an average increase of about $0.32 per unit. A seller who submits a deal today therefore has one day to ship minimally split inventory under the earlier inbound deadline.
Event dates still unstated
The October 8 post does not give the dates of the Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday event itself. Black Friday falls on November 27, 2026, and Cyber Monday on November 30. In 2024, Amazon's Black Friday Week and Cyber Monday event ran from November 21 to December 2, and Amazon said more than 60% of sales came from independent sellers. Whether the 2026 event follows the same 12-day shape is not stated in the notice.
The October event shaped the price ceilings
The deadline lands two weeks after Prime Big Deal Days, which Amazon ran on October 6 and 7 across 22 countries, with deal submissions for that event closing on September 8. The two events interact through pricing. According to the lightning deal explainer, October event prices are excluded from the lookback Amazon uses to set Black Friday Week deal ceilings, so a seller's Prime Big Deal Days discount does not automatically drag down the maximum deal price allowed in November.
Price validation adds another layer. Since April 23, 2026, a seller-submitted List Price must be backed by outside evidence, either recent sales at another retailer or purchases as the Amazon Featured Offer at that price. A List Price that fails validation produces no strike-through display or savings amount. For Prime Exclusive Discounts, a missing reference price hides the deal altogether, and Amazon re-validates discounts every 24 hours, so a deal can become invalid mid-run if the reference price shifts.
None of this appears in the October 8 checklist, yet it bears directly on the second item. A deal flagged as "at-risk" in the dashboard may simply be a deal whose price no longer meets requirements - one of the causes a third-party post on LinkedIn singled out.
A third-party reading of the notice
On October 19, Vanessa Hung, an e-commerce consultant whose LinkedIn headline describes her as an "E-commerce Ecosystem Strategist" focused on Amazon and marketplaces operations, published a post on the same notice. The post is hers, not Amazon's. Its date is inferred: the capture shows it as 15 hours old and the post describes October 20 as "tomorrow." The capture includes no link to Amazon's notice and is cut off partway through its final paragraph.
"Plot twist, today is your last Black Friday planning day," the post opens. Hung writes that she "went through the notice and pulled out the four checks that decide whether a deal runs or gets stuck." She orders them the same way Amazon does, adding detail Amazon's post leaves out.
On account health, Hung writes that "open policy warnings or violations are the first thing to clear," and that "an appeal still waiting on a response is not how you want to enter submission day." The point is relevant because appeals take time. In October 2025, Amazon gave Account Health Assurance sellers a Seller Challenge feature with a 48-hour decision commitment, limited to three challenges per six-month period and only after a standard appeal has failed. Hung was quoted in PPC Land's coverage at the time, calling the feature a sign that Amazon was formalizing seller due process.
On deal health, Hung names "the usual suspects" behind suppressed or at-risk deals: "low inventory, a price that no longer meets deal requirements, or a listing that stopped being buyable." Her post says the cause should be fixed before resubmitting "instead of just recreating the deal." Amazon's post names none of these causes.
On listings, she spells out what "quality requirements" means in practice, according to her reading: "complete titles, images, and bullet points, no suppression alerts, and no missing attributes." She adds that "a catalog glitch loves to show up the moment you build a promotion around that ASIN." The fourth item in her post mentions "payment method, tax information, and deposit account," but the capture ends mid-sentence, so the rest of that paragraph is not available.
Hung's descriptions are her own interpretation. Amazon's notice does not confirm that low inventory or catalog attribute gaps are the main triggers for deal suppression, and it publishes no data on how often deals fail these checks.
Account problems close to deadline
The account health item is not a formality. PPC Land reported in August on a UK seller whose whole account was blocked three days after Amazon reinstated a listing following counterfeit complaints the seller attributed to a coordinated campaign. Amazon's Order Defect Rate threshold is 1%, counting negative feedback, A-to-Z claims and chargebacks, which means a handful of complaints can push a low-volume account over the line. A seller in that position in late October would face the deadline with no clear timeline for resolution.
Sellers selling to businesses face one more layer. Since August 31, Amazon has offered business-only deals to more than 11 million registered business organizations in 10 markets, with a minimum 15% discount during high velocity events, a category that includes Black Friday and Cyber Monday. The October 8 post does not mention business deals.
Why the deadline matters for advertisers
Deals and advertising are bought separately on Amazon, but they meet on the same product pages. A Sponsored Products campaign pointing at an ASIN that loses its deal badge or strike-through price sends paid traffic to a listing at a weaker offer than planned, and the advertiser pays for those clicks regardless. For brands planning holiday media budgets around specific deal prices, a suppressed deal changes the economics of the ad spend attached to it.
The scale of the period explains the pressure. Adobe forecasts US online spending of $12.9 billion on Black Friday and $15.1 billion on Cyber Monday 2026, the latter on track to be the first day American online sales pass $15 billion. Those figures cover all US retail, not Amazon alone, and are forecasts rather than results.
What remains unclear is how much of Amazon's own claim about early placement holds up. The post asserts that early submitters get "better deal visibility and placement," but Amazon has not published how deal slots are allocated. PPC Land's lightning deal explainer notes that Amazon chooses the slot within a 4 to 12 hour window and cites independent research on 2,451 products: deal participation improved category sales rank by about 15%, while the within-product gain over time was only 1.3% to 1.6% and faded after about two weeks. That research did not test the effect of submission timing, which leaves Amazon's early-mover claim unverified.

Summary
Who: Amazon, through a Seller News post for independent sellers, with a separate third-party LinkedIn post by e-commerce consultant Vanessa Hung reacting to the same notice.
What: The deal submission window for Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday events closes, with Amazon listing four checks: Account Health Rating, deal health status, listing quality and payment and tax settings. The post claims early submitters receive better placement but gives no mechanism, figures or fees.
When: Amazon published the reminder on October 8, 2026. The window, open since July 8, closes today, October 20, 2026. Black Friday is November 27 and Cyber Monday November 30.
Where: Amazon's Seller News feed and the Deals dashboard in Seller Central. The post names no markets; the fee and inbound figures cited from PPC Land's earlier coverage apply to the US.
Why: Deals submitted today carry the full $100 upfront fee plus 1.5% of promotional sales, and can still be suppressed over account, price or listing problems. For advertisers, a suppressed deal weakens the offer on product pages that holiday ad campaigns are paying to send traffic to, during days Adobe expects to reach $12.9 billion and $15.1 billion in US online spending.
